transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah—so, I guess what finally pushed me to make the appointment is this thing where I keep getting up when I’m supposed to stay put. Like during sprint planning at work, or even mortgage calls, which are already kind of stressful and boring in a very specific way—I’ll know I should just sit there and listen, and then suddenly I’m up getting water or checking something in the other room.

It’s not like I’m trying to be rude. I just sort of… do it, and then realize afterward that I probably looked distracted.
When you were a child, did you also have trouble staying seated in situations where you were expected to stay in your seat?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, I don’t have, like, a perfect memory of every classroom, but I do remember in elementary school teachers moving my desk around sometimes, or reminding me to sit back down because I’d popped up for some reason.

And I was also the kid who would start talking before I was actually called on, or rush through an assignment even when I knew how to do it. Which is funny because I did fine with the work, mostly, so I don’t think anyone saw it as a huge problem—more like I was just… a lot in the room.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually energetic or wired for several days in a row?

I’m not sure. I mean, I have days where I feel kind of revved up, especially if there’s a release deadline or I’ve had too much coffee—which I know is not exactly what you’re asking, probably.

Several days in a row, though… I don’t think I’ve noticed something clearly like that. My energy is more sort of jumpy and situational, if that makes sense, not like a whole multi-day stretch where I’m unusually wired.
Do you often find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things?

I don’t know that I’d call it excessive. I worry about normal stuff, I guess—work, money things, family, whether I forgot to reply to someone’s email. Actually that email thing reminds me, I have this one thread right now that’s been sitting there and every time I see it I think, “I should really answer that,” and then it becomes this whole little mental tab.

But, sorry—your question was about worrying about lots of things. I’m not sure. It’s not something I’ve really tracked. I wouldn’t say I’m constantly worrying all day, if that’s what you mean.
Do you often pick at your skin in a way that feels hard to stop?

Um… not really, I don’t think. I mean, I’ll mess with a hangnail or something if it’s there, especially if I’m sitting at my desk and notice it, but I don’t think of it as hard to stop.

Actually my hands get dry sometimes from washing them or just winter air, and then I’ll notice little rough spots—sorry, that’s probably more detail than you need. But no, I haven’t noticed skin picking being a real problem for me.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on a task, even when you want to pay attention?

Yeah, I do. Not all the time, but enough that it’s annoying. Like I’ll start reviewing a pull request with every intention of actually reading it carefully, and then a few minutes later I realize I’m just staring at the same chunk of code or the same comment and thinking about, I don’t know, five totally unrelated things.

It happens with paperwork too—like mortgage documents were a nightmare. I’d be trying to pay attention, because obviously those are important, and then I’d catch myself rereading the same paragraph without absorbing it. Then I get frustrated because I do want to focus, it’s not like I don’t care.
When you're trying to focus and your mind drifts, is it usually because you're worrying about something?

Not usually, no. I mean, sometimes I might remember something I need to do, but it’s not mostly worry. It’s more like I start with good intentions—like reviewing a pull request or reading those mortgage documents—and then after a few minutes I realize I’m just staring at the same section and my brain is off on five unrelated things. Like not necessarily bad things, just… random stuff. Then I have to pull myself back and reread it.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or keeping track of what you need to do?

Yeah… organizing is probably one of the things I’m worse at. I don’t mean like my house is a disaster or anything—well, the garage is kind of its own situation, but that’s partly because we kept meaning to put up shelves and then I needed to measure the wall and then the measuring tape disappeared.

But with actual tasks, yeah. My work tickets, notes about home repairs, budget stuff I’m supposed to remember—they end up all over the place. Some are in Slack, some on sticky notes, some buried in email, some in my phone reminders. Then I’ll sit down to do something and spend half the time figuring out where I wrote it down or what I was supposed to be doing in the first place. It’s frustrating because I’m not trying to be careless, it just kind of scatters.
Do you often feel restless or unable to relax, even when there isn’t anything specific you’re worried about?

Yeah, I do. It’s not always like I’m pacing around the room or something obvious like that. Sometimes I’ll look totally calm, like I’m sitting on the couch or at my desk, but inside it feels like there’s this… pressure building? Like I need to get up, or switch to a different thing, or mess with something in my hands.

It’s weird because it can happen even when nothing is actually wrong. Like I’ll be sitting there and my husband will be watching a show, and I’m technically watching too, but part of me is like, okay, can we do something else now? Or I’ll start picking at a label on a bottle or fiddling with my ring, and then suddenly I’ve missed half of what happened. Not because I’m worried, exactly, more like I feel like I’ll crawl out of my skin if I just sit still too long.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation: persistent problems with sustained attention, task organization, distractibility, and losing track of tasks across work and daily life, with childhood onset and current functional impact.
